etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle Dutch snacken (“to snack”).

definitions.definition: An item of food eaten between meals.

quote.citation: 2020 December 2, Paul Bigland, “My weirdest and wackiest Rover yet”, in Rail, page 68:
quote.text: The numbers thin out the further we get from London, so I don't feel guilty when I remove my mask momentarily to scoff some of the snacks I'd bought at Marylebone.

definitions.definition: (slang) A very sexy and attractive person.

quote.citation: 2008, Scott Sherman, First You Fall: A Kevin Connor Mystery, Alyson Publications:
quote.text: Up close, he was a total snack. “That was pretty slick.” “Well.” He cocked his head, “I'm a pretty slick guy.” “I'm Kevin,” I said. “Romeo,” he put out his hand. “You're kidding.”

quote.citation: 2019, Loy A. Webb, The Light, Concord Theatricals, →ISBN, page 22:
quote.text: You were looking like a snack. I was looking like a snack. We were finally going to do what two snacks do... I immediately went into my routine. Covers on. Lights off. But you Mr. Tate...you softly grabbed my hand, kissed it, and turned the lights back on.

quote.citation: 2020, Gena Showalter, Prince of Stone, HQN Books, →ISBN:
quote.text: Her confusion amped up. But so did her attraction. He was a total snack.

quote.citation: 2020 December 2, Paul Bigland, “My weirdest and wackiest Rover yet”, in Rail, page 66:
quote.text: Insult is added to injury when I see the West Coast Railways dining train at the adjacent platform, where guests are sat snacking and drinking wine at a very sociable distance.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: See snatch (transitive verb). Ultimately of the same origin as the word under Etymology 1, but perhaps through a different source.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A share; a part or portion.

quote.citation: 1735 January 13 (Gregorian calendar; indicated as 1734), [Alexander] Pope, An Epistle from Mr. Pope, to Dr. Arbuthnot, London:  […]  J[ohn] Wright for Lawton Gilliver […], →OCLC, page 4, lines 65–66:
quote.text: All my demurrs but double his attacks; / At laſt he vvhiſpers, "Do; and vve go ſnacks."

quote.citation: 1894 July 5, H[erbert] G[eorge] Wells, “The Hammerpond Park Burglary”, in The Stolen Bacillus and Other Incidents, London: Methuen & Co. […], published 1895, →OCLC, pages 216–217:
quote.text: "Have you exhibited very much?" said Young Person in the bar-parlour of the "Coach and Horses," where Mr Watkins was skilfully accumulating local information on the night of his arrival. / "Very little," said Mr Watkins, "just a snack here and there."
